excerpt: Create your first agent with a single command and start building.
Run this command to create a general-purpose agent harness with a local workspace, shell tools, memory, task tracking, web access, and recurring schedules.
Studio is the interface for building, testing, and managing agents, workflows, and tools.
Add Mastra to an existing project, or create a new app with your preferred framework:
Browse [templates](https://mastra.ai/templates) for complete Mastra projects you can clone and adapt.
Moving tool calls to tasks lets the agent keep responding while slow or expensive computations run in the background.
Tools that run as tasks can still use `suspend()` to ask for human input.
Compose typed steps, retries, and branches into production workflows your team can inspect and ship.
Mastra workflows use an intuitive syntax for control flow including .then(), .branch() and .parallel() methods.
Mastra uses storage to remember execution state, so workflows can pause indefinitely and resume where they left off.
Give agents durable context with observational memory, semantic recall, and thread-aware storage.
Coordinate multi-mode agents with shared state, threads, and storage — the same harness that runs Mastra Code.
Register agents and workflows on one Mastra server, run it locally, and deploy the same app to Mastra Cloud.
Inspect every model call, tool call, and handoff from one searchable timeline.
Track latency, cost, model calls, and tool usage across every production agent run.
Score agent runs against repeatable checks before changes reach production.
Capture traces and user feedback into versioned datasets for repeatable evaluation.
Subscribe agent threads to external resources and route webhook or polling events into notification signals.
Mastra's model routing connects to 90+ providers through one standard interface.
MCP servers built with Mastra can be accessed by any system or agent that supports the protocol.
Mastra also provides guardrails to process inputs and outputs, helping prevent prompt injection and sanitize responses.
Mastra includes optional built-in deployers for Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare to automate the deployment process.
Mastra bundles agents and workflows directly into existing React, Next.js and Node.js apps, or ships them as standalone endpoints.
A user who had many problems with LangChain says they are very happy since switching to Mastra.
A user notes only stdio MCP servers were supported by Mastra's MCP client, not SSE. Their workaround is to run a proxy, but they asked for native SSE support.

A commenter disputes the 'open-source' label: Mastra uses the Elastic v2 license, which says 'You may not provide the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service', so they argue it isn't actually open source.

Happy Mastra user: it strikes the right balance between higher-level abstractions and lower-level control when needed. After looking at a handful of other frameworks, Mastra's clarity and ease of use stood out.
A user says they learned everything about how agents work by using Mastra's framework and docs, and that the founders are very hands-on and helpful.

A critic argues Mastra is one of hundreds of similar frameworks. In their view, orchestrating tools with a model is the easy ~5% of the work, and developers still have to fill the other 95% outside the framework's scope.
A commenter says the landing-page workflow example (chained .step().then().after().then().commit()) 'does not exactly spark joy'. They find it a very awkward way to represent even a simple graph.
A commenter objects to Mastra being built on the Vercel AI SDK: 'It started off wrong.'
A user who has been using Mastra for side projects for months calls it 'just phenomenal'.
A commenter notes that with Mastra you're not locked into a model, but you are likely locked into a platform. The convenience just shifts where in the stack the lock-in occurs.
A user building with Mastra for a couple of weeks is loving it. They think building on the Vercel AI SDK was a good decision: the AI SDK is the low-level library and Mastra is the framework.

A user who worked with Mastra for three months found workflows and branching logic clunky for non-LLM, rules-based steps. After a couple weeks of frustration they built their own custom branching workflows, though they still call Mastra best in class for TypeScript.
A user ran through the quickstart, created a 'Friendo' agent and chatted with it. They found the UI nice and the systems cool, but weren't yet sure what to build.

Balancing view from a team user: Mastra is batteries-included and opinionated, and when you don't fit an existing pattern it's hard to stay productive. They repeatedly had to write their own Hono routes and are now rebuilding everything with LangGraph/LangChain, though they credit Mastra's TS-first approach.
A commenter says they don't get Mastra's pricing page because it doesn't seem to list any prices.
A former user who played with Mastra (not Factory) quite a bit describes it as 'a very pleasant experience'.
A commenter points out that Mastra closed its repo to outside contributors and asks whether that pattern is becoming the norm in open source.
A developer says they have been using Mastra in a few agentic projects and will explore Factory further.
Security report: the StepSecurity Threat Intelligence Team identified that multiple Mastra npm packages had been compromised.
